style: Tell this like you're telling a friend something unsettling over coffee. Calm, conversational, understated British voice. Low-key and human, not theatrical: no dramatic pauses, no announcer voice. Pause only briefly where a sentence ends. Short sentences land plainly. Let the facts do the work.

paragraphs.cold: There's a moment in every hospital that nurses are trained to catch. The moment a patient starts to die. It hides in a hundred small readings, and it's easy to miss. In twenty eighteen, a machine learned to catch it first. Google took the medical records of a hundred and fourteen thousand people and fed them to an artificial intelligence. Then it asked one question. Who, in this building, is going to die? It answered with ninety-five per cent accuracy. Earlier than the charts. Earlier than the nurses. Sometimes, earlier than the doctor standing at the bed. The result was published in a medical journal. And it leaves one strange question hanging. Why is an advertising company this good at knowing when you'll die?
paragraphs.act1: At first, this looks like a story about Google moving into healthcare. But the hospital is almost beside the point. Look at what the machine had to do. To see a death coming, it had to be very good at one narrow thing. Take everything known about a person, and work out what happens next. And that's the oldest skill Google has. It's spent twenty years perfecting it on the rest of us. Same engine. Pointed at the final variable.
paragraphs.act2: So how does a company get good enough to forecast a death? It reads all of it. The numbers. The scans. Even the free-text notes a nurse types at three in the morning. Forty-six billion data points, all feeding one set of predictions. And the raw material arrived the way it usually does. A hospital handed Google the records of every patient who came through its doors over seven years, and called them anonymous. But the dates were still attached. So were the doctors' notes. And for a company that already knows where you were on a given afternoon, a dated, annotated medical file doesn't stay anonymous for long. The patients were never asked. No one had to ask them.
